newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek bourse bounces back but crisis not over.
newsitem.headline: Greek bourse bounces back but crisis not over.

text.p: The Athens bourse regained some composure on Friday, closing higher after a week of upheavals which saw trading devastated by the Delta Securities settlement scandal.
Brokers said the crisis, which stopped trade for almost four days, was not over and more tremours could rock the bourse in the weeks ahead.
"We had signs of corruption with the recent crisis at the bourse -- you can't fool everyone all the time," said Phaedon Tamvakakis, managing director of Hambros Hellenic Mutual Funds.
The bourse closed 1.37 percent higher on Friday at 890.39, making up some of Thursday's 3.31 percent plunge. Trade was moderate with volume of 6.06 billion drachmas.
Delta's attempt to pay 2.6 billion drachmas in settlements at the clearing house with bad cheques this month triggered the upheavals at the bourse.

Brokers said the Delta scandal raised the issue of illegal short-selling, often conducted to build up trading volume, and abuse of the clearing house where a large backlog has meant settlement can take weeks instead of the regulated 72 hours.
Even as the bourse rose, more shocks hit the exchange with signs a deal between the government and the Association of Athens Stock Exchange Members (SMEHA) to cover the Delta losses could fall apart.

Four board members of the bourse's guarantee fund, which was to help cover part of the losses, were threatening to quit after accusing the government of trying to get out of the recent deal, the broker sources said.

Should the board resign, it would stop the fund from paying its share of the losses and lead to deadlock. The dispute highlighted the mistrust between the brokers and the government, the sources said.
While brokers fumed, Prime Minister Costas Simitis tried to play down the Delta scandal. His government has been criticized by brokers for failing to react quickly to the crisis.

"The stock market didn't collapse, it was one brokerage that collapsed," he told parliement. A draft bill would introduce new transaction rules, revamp the clearing house and the exchange's guarantee fund, he said.
Despite his reassurances, brokers remained concerned about how far-reaching the scandal would prove to be and noted that government-ordered audits of brokerages could provide more fireworks.
Some brokers predicted a further fall, perhaps as much as five percent, but also suggested it might prove to be a good time to buy.

"After being closed for almost four sessions it is natural to see pent up selling pressure," said broker Gregory Vlahos at Pegasos Securities. "I expect quality stocks will have a 15-20 percent correction on the upside."
ING Barings said in a report that based on a limited poll of 10 brokers and fund managers the market expected another five percent fall.
The poll suggested the market would stabilise at a median 835 points, with answers ranging from 750 to 880.
"We recommend letting the dust settle before taking any action. The risk of another market interruption has subsided, but not disappeared," ING Barings said.
